newsitem.title: CHINA: Beijing gripped with excitement over Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Beijing gripped with excitement over Hong Kong.

text.p: Excitement gripped China's capital on Sunday as tens of thousands flocked for a second night to watch a countdown clock tick away the final hours to the historic return of Hong Kong after 156 years of British colonial rule.

As many as 200,000 people, hoping to share in the thrill of the moment, poured into Tiananmen Square in the heart of the capital late on Sunday, clogging streets, snarling traffic and lending a carnival atmosphere to the city, officials said.
Zhu Po, a worker, bowed in silent prayer to the portrait of Chairman Mao Zedong hanging above Tiananmen Gate, but said Mao should not have the credit for the return of Hong Kong.
"I think we would firstly thank Deng Xiaoping for that," she said, referring to his negotiations with Britain that led to the treaty on Hong Kong's return in 1984.
Many people sat on street corners, playing cards, chatting excitedly and revelling in the run-up to the end of colonial rule at the stroke of midnight on June 30.
"We aren't invited to the official celebrations so this is our chance to enjoy the return of Hong Kong," said a student as he sat with his classmates on a kerbside near the square.

About 100,000 people are expected to jam into Tiananmen Square to watch the huge digital clock mark the end of colonial rule. But all of them will be on the official guest list, and for those left out, Sunday night was the time to party.
In front of the clock, crowds cheered as each 1,000 seconds ticked away in the countdown to the midnight handover.
For China, the day marks the end of a national humiliation after British gunboats humbled a weak imperial China in the Opium War.
Britain claimed Hong Kong as its prize in the 1842 Treaty of Nanjing, one of the agreements since referred to as the "unequal treaties".
High above China's capital, a blimp proclaims the impending recovery of the territory, bearing the message "Celebrate the Return of Hong Kong".

Down below, Chinese flags flutter across the city while banners stream across pedestrian bridges and on street corners, shouting: "Wash away 100 years of national shame" and "A better tomorrow for Hong Kong".

A daily pilgrimage of city residents and tourists ends at Tiananmen Square where workmen raced against time to get ready for the ceremony, children flew kites or roller-skated around the mausoleum of Chairman Mao Zedong.
"Take off your glasses," implored one young woman, pointing a camera at her husband. "Don't move."
Her husband confided they were newlyweds on their honeymoon, in Beijing to stand on the spot where the ceremony will be held.
"We just got married," he said. "It's a great time to be here and a great time to start out in life together."
Not all were excited. Zhao Gengshen, a 17-year-old student, said he was dragged to the square by his girlfriend.
"I am not so interested in Hong Kong, I'm too tired from studying," he said, adding that his exams were on July 2.
A vendor of paper Chinese and Hong Kong flags did a brisk trade, selling a pair for four yuan ($0.48).
"It was only three yuan yesterday," said a somewhat disgruntled customer.
"We're running out of them," came the laconic reply.
